No direct controlled comparison was found for this exact five-item exponential pool against last-item-only, uniform pooling, and learned decay. SASRec’s published results support adaptive attention, not this augmentation ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781)). Mathematically, normalized exp(-age), ages 0–4, assigns approximately 63.6%, 23.4%, 8.6%, 3.2%, 1.2%; the latest two items receive 87%. Thus, improvement alone does not establish repeated-interest modeling. Recommended ablations: identical SASRec plus no pool, last-item embedding, uniform five-item pool, fixed exponential pool, and learned nonnegative decay; hold fusion, scaling, dropout, training, and validation candidates constant.

Implementation guidance: at every position t, pool only embeddings at t through t−4, excluding padding and renormalizing valid weights; return zero for empty windows. Predict item t+1, never include its embedding. Original SASRec zeroes padding embeddings, scales input item embeddings by sqrt(d), adds positions, applies dropout, and masks padded states; output item embeddings remain unscaled ([embedding code](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kang205/SASRec/master/modules.py), [model code](https://github.com/kang205/SASRec/blob/master/model.py)). The added pool has no canonical scaling/dropout convention: specify whether it uses raw or scaled embeddings, apply consistent regularization across ablations, and disable dropout during evaluation.

For shortcut dependence, supplement validation HR@10 with separately trained last-item baselines, pool-branch removal, and inference perturbations that remove the newest item or older context; report category-level effects. These are proposed diagnostics. Published HRLI measures how often the last observed item appears in full-catalog top-K; SASRec reached approximately 0.99 on Beauty/Sports ([study](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.09722v1)). HRLI requires retaining seen items in a separate diagnostic ranking; unseen-only recommendations make it zero by construction. High HRLI flags recency dependence but does not prove harmful shortcut learning.
